explanations.answer: The sufferings are not comparable to the glory
explanations.explanation: Paul, the apostle writing to the believers in Rome, says it plainly: "I consider that our present sufferings are not comparable to the glory that will be revealed in us." (Romans 8:18) Not comparable. These two don't even fit on the same scale, friend. I think that's the kind of math that lets a tired person breathe a little.

explanations.answer: The sufferings are about equal to the glory
explanations.explanation: Equal would mean a fair trade, and Paul never says that. He says the sufferings are "not comparable to the glory that will be revealed in us." (Romans 8:18) That's like setting one crumb on the scale against a whole batch and being shocked at which side drops. The glory is the batch, friend.

explanations.answer: The sufferings will last longer than the glory
explanations.explanation: Paul never says how long either one lasts. He calls them "present sufferings" and says they are "not comparable to the glory that will be revealed in us." (Romans 8:18) His weighing is about how the two measure up, and there's no stopwatch in it. So don't go hunting for a timer that isn't there.

Right on the money. Paul writes, "The creation waits in eager expectation for the revelation of the sons of God." (Romans 8:19) Creation is leaning forward in its chair, friend. It's waiting on the sons of God to be revealed.

I get why angels come to mind, since they show up in the Bible a lot. But they're not in this verse at all. Paul says the creation is waiting "for the revelation of the sons of God." (Romans 8:19) Angels are off the guest list for this one.

The prophets don't come up in this verse, friend. Paul says the creation "waits in eager expectation for the revelation of the sons of God." (Romans 8:19) It's the sons of God being revealed that creation is watching for. Good guess, wrong tray.

True. Paul says, "For the creation was subjected to futility, not by its own will, but because of the One who subjected it, in hope…" (Romans 8:20) Creation didn't choose this, friend. And notice that little word at the end: hope. The sentence doesn't stop at futility.

That one's actually true, friend. Paul says the creation "was subjected to futility, not by its own will, but because of the One who subjected it, in hope…" (Romans 8:20) So creation didn't choose its own futility. I know, I read it twice myself and my mustache needed a minute.

explanations.answer: It will be set free from its decay
explanations.explanation: That's the hope. Paul says "the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to decay and brought into the glorious freedom of the children of God." (Romans 8:21) Free from bondage, friend, and brought into glorious freedom. Creation gets in on the good news too.

explanations.answer: It will be returned to the garden
explanations.explanation: A garden is a lovely picture, but Paul doesn't mention one here. He says the creation "will be set free from its bondage to decay and brought into the glorious freedom of the children of God." (Romans 8:21) The hope is freedom from decay. I'd rather stick to what he actually wrote.

explanations.answer: It will be at rest from all storms
explanations.explanation: Storms never come up in this verse, friend. Paul says the creation "will be set free from its bondage to decay and brought into the glorious freedom of the children of God." (Romans 8:21) The word is freedom, and it's tied to decay. A little rest sounds nice, but that's not what he says.

Not quite, friend. Paul says, "We know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until the present time." (Romans 8:22) Until the present time means it was still going when he wrote. The groaning hadn't stopped.

False is right. Paul says the whole creation "has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until the present time." (Romans 8:22) So as he writes, the groaning is still going. Childbirth pains, friend, and everybody knows those are leading somewhere.

Yes! Paul says believers "groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for our adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies." (Romans 8:23) He doesn't leave adoption hanging. He tells you what it is, and it includes our bodies. I'll admit, my old stamper body would love that news.

explanations.answer: A rest from all their labor
explanations.explanation: Rest sounds wonderful after a long day, but that's not what Paul says here. He says believers wait eagerly for "our adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies." (Romans 8:23) The adoption is spelled out right in the verse. Rest isn't mentioned.

explanations.answer: A home in the promised land
explanations.explanation: The promised land is a big theme elsewhere in the Bible, but it's not in this verse. Paul says believers wait for "our adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies." (Romans 8:23) He defines adoption right there, friend. It's the redemption of our bodies.

Paul says the opposite, friend. He writes, "hope that is seen is no hope at all." (Romans 8:24) Then he asks, "Who hopes for what he can already see?" Nobody stands at the oven hoping for a cookie that's already in their hand.

False, and you're right. Paul says, "hope that is seen is no hope at all. Who hopes for what he can already see?" (Romans 8:24) Hope is for what's still ahead. Once you can see it, you're not hoping anymore, you're holding it.

Patiently is the word. Paul says, "But if we hope for what we do not yet see, we wait for it patiently." (Romans 8:25) Waiting patiently for something unseen is hard, friend. I should know, I did a lot of it in a dusty drawer.

I know that kind of waiting well, with the knuckle chewing and the pacing. But Paul says, "But if we hope for what we do not yet see, we wait for it patiently." (Romans 8:25) The word is patiently, not nervously. Paul puts hope and patience together.

Brief waiting would be nice, wouldn't it? But Paul doesn't say how long it takes. He says, "But if we hope for what we do not yet see, we wait for it patiently." (Romans 8:25) A patient wait is what he describes, and it says nothing about how short it is.

Paul says the opposite, friend. He writes, "we do not know how we ought to pray." (Romans 8:26) That's a pretty honest thing to put in a letter. It tells you the apostle himself included that struggle in the "we."

False is right. Paul says, "For we do not know how we ought to pray…" (Romans 8:26) He says it about "we," so he's counting himself in. Plenty of us run out of words, and that's nothing to be ashamed of.

explanations.answer: With groans too deep for words
explanations.explanation: That's it. Paul says, "the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groans too deep for words." (Romans 8:26) When we're out of words, the Spirit isn't. His groans are deeper than anything we could put into a sentence.

explanations.answer: With songs of praise in heaven
explanations.explanation: Songs of praise are a beautiful thing, but Paul doesn't say that here. He says the Spirit "intercedes for us with groans too deep for words." (Romans 8:26) It's groans, friend, and they go deeper than any words we've got.

explanations.answer: With the words of the prophets
explanations.explanation: The prophets aren't in this verse, friend. Paul says "the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groans too deep for words." (Romans 8:26) The whole point is that these groans are beyond words. Even the best words aren't what he's describing.

True. Paul says, "the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God." (Romans 8:27) So the Spirit isn't guessing and He isn't winging it. He's praying right along the will of God, even when we've got nothing.

That's actually true, friend. Paul says, "the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God." (Romans 8:27) The Spirit's praying lines up with God's will. No need to worry that He's off script.

True. Paul says, "And we know that God works all things together for the good of those who love Him, who are called according to His purpose." (Romans 8:28) Notice who it's for: those who love Him, who are called according to His purpose. And he says all things, friend, not some things.

It's true, friend. Paul writes, "And we know that God works all things together for the good of those who love Him, who are called according to His purpose." (Romans 8:28) It's God doing the working, and it's for those who love Him. That's a big promise, so I read it slowly.

explanations.answer: To be conformed to the image of His Son
explanations.explanation: Yes. Paul says, "For those God foreknew, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son…" (Romans 8:29) The goal is to look like the Son. Not a title and not a job, friend, but the image of Jesus.

explanations.answer: To be made servants in His Son's kingdom
explanations.explanation: Serving is a good thing, but it's not what this verse says. Paul says those God foreknew, "He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son…" (Romans 8:29) The goal here is being shaped into the image of the Son. Servants aren't mentioned.

explanations.answer: To be set as priests in His holy temple
explanations.explanation: Priests and temples are big in other parts of the Bible, but this verse doesn't mention them. Paul says God predestined those He foreknew "to be conformed to the image of His Son…" (Romans 8:29) That's the destination here. It's about becoming like the Son.

Brothers is the word. Paul says it's "so that He would be the firstborn among many brothers." (Romans 8:29) The Son isn't alone at the front of the line, friend. He's the firstborn with many brothers behind Him.

Kings sounds grand, but that's not what Paul writes. He says it's "so that He would be the firstborn among many brothers." (Romans 8:29) It's a family word, friend. The Son is the firstborn, and the many are brothers.
Angels aren't in this verse. Paul says the Son would be "the firstborn among many brothers." (Romans 8:29) It's a family word again, friend. Many brothers, with the Son as the firstborn.

That's the last link. Paul says, "those He justified, He also glorified." (Romans 8:30) Called, justified, glorified. And look at it, friend: Paul says it as one unbroken chain, and glorified is where it lands.

Tested isn't part of Paul's chain here. He writes, "those He justified, He also glorified." (Romans 8:30) The chain ends at glorified. I do like a good test run on a new batch, but that's not what this verse says.
Being sent out is a good thing, but it's not where this chain ends. Paul says, "those He justified, He also glorified." (Romans 8:30) Glorified is the last link, friend. Nothing comes after it.
